title: Mini-cadence staffing auction and mandatory scope anchor
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Mid-cycle scope creep and uneven staffing requests create bursts that derail higher-priority initiatives. Proposal: Run a 3-cycle experiment that introduces a lightweight "mini-cadence" (6-week micro-window inside existing cycle cadence) where teams bid staffing credit for short, high-impact deliverables via a transparent auction. Each bid must include a mandatory scope anchor: a 20% down-scope fallback that can be executed if full staffing doesn't clear. Goal: improve predictability, reduce fire drills, and surface real tradeoffs between velocity and priority across product, eng, and design.
acceptance_criteria: Auction mechanism prototype implemented in the cycle-planning spreadsheet and lightweight web UI (alpha)
At least 6 teams submit bids during the pilot mini-cadence window for Cycle 2026-W11
Mechanism enforces mandatory 20% scope-anchor text on every bid and validates it during submission
Post-pilot retrospective shows measurable reduction in unplanned mid-cycle scope additions (target: -30% compared to prior 3 cycles)
Operational metrics captured: number of bids, cleared bids, staff-hours allocated, rework due to scope-cuts, and PM/Eng satisfaction survey
proposal_notes: Design: keep bidding UI intentionally simple (title, ask in FTE-weeks, scope anchor description, risk/QA notes)
Auction rules: teams get credits based on historical burn rate + strategic multipliers assigned by PM leads
Clearing logic: highest strategic score wins until credits exhausted; ties resolved by leadership quick-review panel
decisions: Run pilot for three mini-cadence windows (2026-W11, W17, W23)
Mandatory 20% scope-anchor on every bid — bids missing this are considered invalid
Use conservative credit calculation to avoid over-allocation (credits = 0.8 * historical average burn for team)
Initial auction UI will be a single-page web app + Google Sheet mirror for auditability
tradeoffs: Pros: forces explicit scope clarity and creates visibility of tradeoffs; encourages PMs to prioritize ruthlessly
Cons: adds one extra lightweight process and may be seen as bureaucracy; risk of gaming credit multipliers by teams
Mitigation: keep process time-boxed, publish transparent scoring rubric, and monitor for gaming signals
